      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Depression</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Dysthymic <span class="qt3">Disorder</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Clinical <span class="qt1">depression</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Major</span> <span class="qt2">depressive <span class="qt3">disorder</span></span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Unipolar <span class="qt1">depression</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt1">depression</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Depression</span> is more than a feeling of being sad or irritable for a few days. It's a serious mood <span class="qt3">disorder</span>. As one of the most common mental <span class="qt3">disorders</span> in the United States, <span class="qt1">depression</span> can affect how you think, feel, and your everyday life. You may not know why you feel this way, but even basic daily activities such as sleeping, eating, or working may become difficult. <span class="qt1">Depression</span> often needs long-term treatment but getting help at the earliest sign of a problem can help manage your symptoms.</p>What are the different types of <span class="qt1">depression</span>?<p>The most common types of <span class="qt1">depression</span> are <span class="qt0">major</span> <span class="qt1">depression</span> and persistent <span class="qt2">depressive <span class="qt3">disorder</span></span>.</p><ul><li><span class="qt0">Major</span> <span class="qt1">depression</span> symptoms include a depressed mood or a loss of interest. Symptoms affect your daily activities and last for at least two weeks.</li><li>Persistent <span class="qt2">depressive <span class="qt3">disorder</span></span> (also called dysthymia or dysthymic <span class="qt3">disorder</span>) has less severe depressive symptoms, but they last longer, usually for at least two years.</li></ul><p>Other types of <span class="qt1">depression</span> can include:</p><ul><li>Seasonal affective <span class="qt3">disorder</span> comes and goes with the seasons. It usually starts in late fall and early winter and goes away during the spring and summer.</li><li>Bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span> is sometimes called manic <span class="qt1">depression</span>. This mood <span class="qt3">disorder</span> can cause intense mood swings.</li><li><span class="qt1">Depression</span> with symptoms of psychosis is a severe form of <span class="qt1">depression</span> that also has delusions (false beliefs) or hallucinations (seeing, hearing, or feeling something that isn't there).</li></ul>What causes <span class="qt1">depression</span>?<p>There are a variety of things that may cause <span class="qt1">depression</span>, including genetic, biological, environmental, and psychological factors. <span class="qt1">Depression</span> can happen at any age and can affect anyone, but it's more common in women. This is often due to the physical and hormonal changes that women have during menstruation, pregnancy, the postpartum period, and menopause. Other mental <span class="qt3">disorders</span> or chronic medical conditions such as diabetes, cancer, or heart <span class="qt4">disease</span> may occur with <span class="qt1">depression</span>. This may make the chronic condition or <span class="qt1">depression</span> worse.</p><p>In some cases, there is no clear cause for <span class="qt1">depression</span>.</p>Who is at risk of <span class="qt1">depression</span>?<p>You may be at a higher risk of <span class="qt1">depression</span> if you have a close relative who has it or another mental health <span class="qt3">disorder</span>. Going through trauma or stressful life events may raise your risk even more.</p>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt1">depression</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Depression</span> doesn't look the same on everyone. The type and number of symptoms of <span class="qt1">depression</span> can vary and don't always appear like sadness. <span class="qt1">Depression</span> may affect you differently based on your:</p><ul><li>Age. The symptoms of <span class="qt1">depression</span> may be different in a child, who may appear more irritable than sad. Teens may act out or have excessive sleepiness. The symptoms for an older adult may not be as obvious as other age groups.</li><li>Sex. Men often show symptoms and coping behaviors differently than women. Rather than sad, men may appear angry or irritable.</li><li>Medical conditions. Some medicines and medical conditions may cause symptoms that look like <span class="qt1">depression</span>. Chronic conditions may make <span class="qt1">depression</span> worse.</li></ul><p>Symptoms of <span class="qt1">depression</span> are ongoing and affect your day-to-day life. They can include:</p><ul><li>Feeling sad or "empty"</li><li>Losing interest in favorite activities</li><li>Overeating, or not wanting to eat at all</li><li>Sleeping too much, or not enough</li><li>Feeling very tired</li><li>Feeling hopeless, irritable, anxious, or guilty</li><li>Having aches and pains, headaches, cramps, or digestive problems</li><li>Having thoughts of death or suicide</li><li>Changing moods or behaviors</li><li>Increasing use of alcohol or drugs</li><li>Isolating from family and friends</li></ul>How is <span class="qt1">depression</span> diagnosed?<p>If you think you have <span class="qt1">depression</span>, talk to your health care provider or a mental health provider. To be diagnosed with <span class="qt1">depression</span>, your provider may use many tools:</p><ul><li>A medical history will include asking about your symptoms and family history. To be diagnosed with <span class="qt1">depression</span>, your symptoms must occur most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks. One of the symptoms must be a depressed mood or a loss of interest in most activities.</li><li>Medical tests may be done to rule out other medical conditions. Certain medicines and medical conditions (such as viruses or thyroid <span class="qt3">disorders</span>) may cause symptoms like <span class="qt1">depression</span>.</li><li>A physical exam to make sure another issue isn't causing your symptoms.</li><li>A mental health evaluation by your provider or a mental health provider.</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt1">depression</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Depression</span> may need long-term treatment. Most treatments include medicines and/or psychotherapy (talk therapy):</p><ul><li>Medicines such as antidepressants may help control your symptoms. You may need to try several medicines to find which works best for you. Medicine may take time to work and can have side effects. Don't stop taking your medicine without first talking with your provider. Contact your provider if you have any concerns about side effects from the medicine.</li><li>Psychotherapy (talk therapy) under the care of a mental health provider can help you recognize and change troubling emotions, thoughts, and behaviors. This may be done one-on-one or in a group setting. It can give you and your family support, education, skills, and coping strategies.</li><li>Light therapy has been shown to be effective for seasonal affective <span class="qt3">disorder</span> (SAD).</li><li>Other treatments options may be considered if treatment isn't working or if <span class="qt1">depression</span> is severe. These may include:
	<ul><li>Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is a brain stimulation procedure that uses a mild electric current when you are under general anesthesia. ECT is most often used for severe <span class="qt1">depression</span> that is not getting better with other treatments.</li><li>Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a brain stimulation procedure that uses magnetic waves to relieve <span class="qt1">depression</span>. It's not as powerful as ECT, but with rTMS, you don't need anesthesia. It also has a low risk of negative effects on your memory and thinking.</li></ul>
</li></ul>Can <span class="qt1">depression</span> be prevented?<p>Most cases of <span class="qt1">depression</span> can't be prevented, but healthy lifestyle changes can have long-term benefits for your mental health. These can include:</p><ul><li>Getting regular exercise</li><li>Having a consistent sleep schedule</li><li>Controlling stress</li></ul><p>If you, or someone you love is depressed, see your provider or a mental health provider. It's important to get treatment at the earliest sign of a problem.</p><p>If you or someone you know has thoughts of hurting themselves or attempting suicide, get help right away. If it is an emergency, dial 911.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Mental Health</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/seasonalaffectivedisorder.html">
      <content name="title">Seasonal Affective <span class="qt3">Disorder</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">SAD</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Major</span> <span class="qt2">depressive <span class="qt3">disorder</span></span> with seasonal pattern</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Seasonal <span class="qt1">depression</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Seasonal mood <span class="qt3">disorder</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Seasonal affective <span class="qt3">disorder</span> (SAD) is a type of <span class="qt1">depression</span> that comes and goes with the seasons. It usually starts in the late fall and early winter and goes away during the spring and summer. Some people do have episodes of <span class="qt1">depression</span> that start in the spring or summer, but that is a lot less common. Symptoms of SAD may include:</p><ul><li>Sadness</li><li>Gloomy outlook</li><li>Feeling hopeless, worthless, and irritable</li><li>Loss of interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy</li><li>Low energy</li><li>Difficulty sleeping or oversleeping</li><li>Carbohydrate cravings and weight gain</li><li>Thoughts of death or suicide</li></ul><p>SAD is more common in women, young people, and those who live far from the equator. You are also more likely to have SAD if you or your family members have <span class="qt1">depression</span>.</p><p>The exact causes of SAD are unknown. Researchers have found that people with SAD may have an imbalance of serotonin, a brain chemical that affects your mood. Their bodies also make too much melatonin, a hormone that regulates sleep, and not enough vitamin D.</p><p>The main treatment for SAD is light therapy. The idea behind light therapy is to replace the sunshine that you miss during the fall and winter months. You sit in front of a light therapy box every morning to get daily exposure to bright, artificial light. But some people with SAD do not respond to light therapy alone. Antidepressant medicines and talk therapy can reduce SAD symptoms, either alone or combined with light therapy.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Mental Health</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/bipolardisorder.html">
      <content name="title">Bipolar <span class="qt3">Disorder</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Bi-Polar <span class="qt3">Disorder</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Manic-Depressive <span class="qt4">Illness</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Manic <span class="qt1">depression</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span>?<p>Bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span> is a mood <span class="qt3">disorder</span> that can cause intense mood swings:</p><ul><li>Sometimes you may feel extremely "up," elated, irritable, or energized. This is called a manic episode.</li><li>Other times you may feel "down," sad, indifferent, or hopeless. This is called a depressive episode.</li><li>You may have both manic and depressive symptoms together. This is called a mixed episode.</li></ul><p>Along with mood swings, bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span> causes changes in behavior, energy levels, and activity levels.</p><p>Bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span> used to be called other names, including manic <span class="qt1">depression</span> and manic-<span class="qt2">depressive <span class="qt3">disorder</span></span>.</p>What are the types of bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span>?<p>There are three main types of bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span>:</p><ul><li>Bipolar I <span class="qt3">disorder</span> involves manic episodes that last at least 7 days or manic symptoms so severe that you need immediate hospital care. Depressive episodes are also common. Those often last at least two weeks. This type of bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span> can also involve mixed episodes.</li><li>Bipolar II <span class="qt3">disorder</span> involves depressive episodes. But instead of full-blown manic episodes, there are episodes of hypomania. Hypomania is a less severe version of mania.</li><li>Cyclothymic <span class="qt3">disorder</span>, or cyclothymia, also involves hypomanic and depressive symptoms. But they are not as intense or as long-lasting as hypomanic or depressive episodes. The symptoms usually last for at least two years in adults and for one year in children and teenagers.</li></ul><p>With any of these types, having four or more episodes of mania or <span class="qt1">depression</span> in a year is called "rapid cycling."</p>What causes bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span>?<p>The exact cause of bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span> is unknown. Several factors likely play a role in the <span class="qt3">disorder</span>. They include genetics, brain structure and function, and your environment.</p>Who is at risk for bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span>?<p>You are at higher risk for bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span> if you have a close relative who has it. Going through trauma or stressful life events may raise this risk even more.</p>What are the symptoms of bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span>?<p>The symptoms of bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span> can vary. But they involve mood swings known as mood episodes:</p><ul><li>The symptoms of a manic episode can include:
     <ul><li>Feeling very up, high, or elated</li><li>Feeling jumpy or wired, more active than usual</li><li>Having a very short temper or seeming extremely irritable</li><li>Having racing thoughts and talking very fast</li><li>Needing less sleep</li><li>Feeling like you are unusually important, talented, or powerful</li><li>Doing risky things that show poor judgment, such as eating and drinking too much, spending or giving away a lot of money, or having reckless sex</li></ul> 
</li><li>The symptoms of a depressive episode can include:
    <ul><li>Feeling very sad, hopeless, or worthless</li><li>Feeling lonely or isolating yourself from others</li><li>Talking very slowly, feeling like you have nothing to say, or forgetting a lot</li><li>Having little energy</li><li>Sleeping too much</li><li>Eating too much or too little</li><li>Lack of interest in your usual activities and being unable to do even simple things</li><li>Thinking about death or suicide</li></ul>
</li><li>The symptoms of a mixed episode include both manic and depressive symptoms together. For example, you may feel very sad, empty, or hopeless, while at the same time feeling extremely energized.</li></ul><p>Some people with bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span> may have milder symptoms. For example, you may have hypomania instead of mania. With hypomania, you may feel very good and find that you can get a lot done. You may not feel like anything is wrong. But your family and friends may notice your mood swings and changes in activity levels. They may realize that your behavior is unusual for you. After the hypomania, you might have severe <span class="qt1">depression</span>.</p><p>Your mood episodes may last a week or two or sometimes longer. During an episode, symptoms usually occur every day for most of the day.</p>How is bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span> diagnosed?<p>To diagnose bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span>, your health care provider may use many tools:</p><ul><li>A physical exam.</li><li>A medical history, which will include asking about your symptoms, lifetime history, experiences, and family history.</li><li>Medical tests to rule out other conditions.</li><li>A mental health evaluation. Your provider may do the evaluation or may refer you to a mental health specialist to get one.</li></ul>What are the treatments for bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span>?<p>Treatment can help many people, including those with the most severe forms of bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span>. The main treatments for bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span> include medicines, psychotherapy, or both:</p><ul><li>Medicines can help control the symptoms of bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span>. You may need to try several different medicines to find which one works best for you. Some people need to take more than one medicine. It's important to take your medicine consistently. Don't stop taking it without first talking with your provider.  Contact your provider if you have any concerns about side effects from the medicines.</li><li>Psychotherapy (talk therapy) can help you recognize and change troubling emotions, thoughts, and behaviors. It can give you and your family support, education, skills, and coping strategies. There are several different types of psychotherapy that may help with bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span>.</li><li>Other treatment options include:
    <ul><li>Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), a brain stimulation procedure that can help relieve symptoms. It uses a mild electric current and is done while you are under general anesthesia. ECT is most often used for severe bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span> that is not getting better with other treatments. It may also be used when someone needs a treatment that will work more quickly than medicines. This might be when a person has a high risk of suicide or is catatonic (unresponsive).</li><li>Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), a brain stimulation procedure that uses magnetic waves to relieve <span class="qt1">depression</span>. It is not as powerful as ECT, but with rTMS, you don't need general anesthesia. It also has a low risk of negative effects on your memory and thinking.
  </li><li>Light therapy has been shown to be effective for seasonal affective <span class="qt3">disorder</span> (SAD). Many people with bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span> also find that their <span class="qt1">depression</span> gets worse during certain seasons, usually in the fall and winter. Light therapy may help with their symptoms.</li><li>Healthy lifestyle changes, such as getting regular exercise, having a consistent sleep schedule, and keeping a mood journal, can also help with your symptoms.</li></ul>    
</li></ul><p>Bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span> is a lifelong <span class="qt4">illness</span>. But long-term, ongoing treatment can help manage your symptoms and enable you to live a healthy, successful life.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Mental Health</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/psychoticdisorders.html">
      <content name="title">Psychotic <span class="qt3">Disorders</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Psychoses</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Psychotic <span class="qt3">disorders</span> are severe mental <span class="qt3">disorders</span> that cause abnormal thinking and perceptions. People with psychoses lose touch with reality. Two of the main symptoms are delusions and hallucinations. Delusions are false beliefs, such as thinking that someone is plotting against you or that the TV is sending you secret messages. Hallucinations are false perceptions, such as hearing, seeing, or feeling something that is not there.</p><p>Schizophrenia is one type of psychotic <span class="qt3">disorder</span>. People with bipolar <span class="qt3">disorder</span> may also have psychotic symptoms. Other problems that can cause psychosis include alcohol and some drugs, brain tumors, brain infections, and stroke.</p><p>Treatment depends on the cause of the psychosis. It might involve drugs to control symptoms and talk therapy. Hospitalization is an option for serious cases where a person might be dangerous to himself or others.</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/fatigue.html">
      <content name="title">Fatigue</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Tiredness</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Weariness</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is fatigue?<p>Fatigue is a feeling of weariness, tiredness, or lack of energy. It can interfere with your usual daily activities. Fatigue can be a normal response to physical activity, emotional stress, boredom, or lack of sleep. But sometimes it can be a sign of a mental or physical condition. If you have been feeling tired for weeks, contact your health care provider. They can help you find out what's causing your fatigue and recommend ways to relieve it.</p>What causes fatigue?<p>Fatigue itself is not a <span class="qt4">disease</span>; it's a symptom. It can have many different causes, including pregnancy and various medical problems, treatments, and lifestyle habits such as:</p><ul><li>Medical problems:<ul><li>Chronic (long-lasting) <span class="qt4">diseases</span> such as diabetes, <span class="qt4">COPD</span> (chronic obstructive pulmonary <span class="qt4">disease</span>), and heart, liver, kidney and thyroid <span class="qt4">diseases</span></li><li>Untreated pain and <span class="qt4">diseases</span> like fibromyalgia</li><li>Anemia</li><li>Infections</li><li>Parkinson's <span class="qt4">disease</span></li><li>Sleep apnea and other sleep <span class="qt3">disorders</span></li><li>Recent stroke</li><li>Mental <span class="qt3">disorders</span> such as <span class="qt1">depression</span> and anxiety</li></ul></li><li>Treatments:<ul><li>Cancer treatments such as chemotherapy, radiation, and bone marrow transplants</li><li>Recovering from <span class="qt0">major</span> surgery</li><li>Taking certain medicines, such as antidepressants, antihistamines, and medicines for nausea and pain</li></ul></li><li>Lifestyle habits:<ul><li>Not getting enough sleep</li><li>Staying up too late</li><li>Drinking too much alcohol</li><li>Substance use</li><li>Having too much caffeine (which can keep you from getting a good night's sleep)</li><li>Getting too little or too much exercise</li></ul></li></ul><p>Overwhelming fatigue is part of a <span class="qt3">disorder</span> called myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS). The fatigue caused by this <span class="qt3">disorder</span> is different from a tired feeling that goes away after you rest. Instead, the fatigue in ME/CFS lasts a long time, does not get better with rest, and limits your ability to do ordinary daily activities.</p>What can I do to manage fatigue?<p>If you've had fatigue that does not get better after several weeks, call your provider. They will ask questions about your sleep, daily activities, appetite, and exercise. They will likely do a physical exam and order lab tests. Once they decide on a diagnosis, they can tell you what treatments might help.</p><p>You can also make some lifestyle changes to feel less tired:</p><ul><li>Get regular physical activity</li><li>Improve your sleep habits</li><li>Stop smoking (if you smoke), since smoking is linked to many <span class="qt4">diseases</span> that can cause fatigue</li><li>Manage stress</li><li>Eat a healthy diet and avoid alcohol</li></ul><p>It also may be helpful for you to keep a fatigue diary. This can help you find patterns throughout the day, such as when you feel more tired and when you have more energy. It can also help you plan for activities that may give you more energy.</p><p>NIH: National Institute on Aging</p></content>
